demos.heading: Before you run anything: set up the shell
demos.purpose: DocuMind can answer a tenant's questions from four stores: its own Vector Search index (the ANN tier), the Firestore rung beneath it, or two managed mirrors, Vertex AI RAG Engine and Vertex AI Search. make up pins acme to RAG Engine and zeta to Vertex AI Search so every store the course teaches is exercised. A managed store holds the text of every current version, but not the kit's addresses: its citations come back with ids like acme:acme_497809ff...#rag-532341da71fe, a page of null even for a PDF, and stages.retrieval_backend: rag_engine. This lesson is about the kit's own rows, so point acme at them for the duration and put the pin back at the end. Module 2 compares the four stores; Module 7 studies the mirrors.

demos.heading: make improve: one rule from the row
demos.purpose: The target. make improve runs one script two ways. Without REVIEWER= it proposes a rule from ROW=. With REVIEWER= it accepts the proposal. IMPROVE_ARGS passes --prompt-only or --rule. The target has no guard-project, because accepting is offline and a model's proposal stops without PROJECT. First, what the proposer would be sent. --prompt-only prints the request and stops, at Rs 0. It contains the rules as they are served today, the dated line, your row, and the phrases a rule may not contain. Before any of that, the row's figures and anchors are checked against the tenant's documents. A row whose golden row could never pass stops at that check, and costs nothing: Then the proposal. One call to gemini-3.1-pro-preview on the global endpoint, at its default thinking, under a JSON schema that asks for rule and why. Timeouts, 429s and server errors are retried with backoff, up to 4 attempts. The reply goes through the same check before anything is written. A rule that passes goes to evals/reports/proposal.json, which is gitignored, with the row, the version it builds on, and the call's tokens and rupees at list price. Here is the shape of that output, from the kit's own code with a scripted proposer standing in for the model. That is how the kit's test runs it. The request is the one --prompt-only printed above, and the reply is the page's example rule. The token counts are the kit test's: 1,800 in and 1,360 out, 1,200 of them thinking, which is billed as output. Propose the kit test's own bad rule as yours, with --rule. No model is called. The check finds "never refuse", which undoes rule 3, refuses the rule and writes nothing, and make reports the failure.

You review one answer from DocuMind, a retrieval-grounded assistant, and propose one rule for its prompt.

The prompt's rules today (v3), which every answer starts with:
<<<
You are DocuMind, a retrieval-grounded assistant.
Rules:
1. Answer ONLY from the numbered context below. Never invent sources.
2. Cite using [N] where N is the chunk number. Multiple chunks: [1,2].
3. If the context does not contain the answer, set answerable=false and say so.
4. Keep answers under 300 words unless asked for more.
5. A quote is the clause that answers - at most twenty-five words, never a whole section.
>>>
When a source in the context carries an effective date, this line follows them too:
<<<
6. Some sources carry an effective date. Where sources disagree, follow the one with the latest effective date, cite it, and say which source you followed and from when it applies.
>>>

The answer that went wrong:
- tenant: acme
- question: I am still on probation. If I resign now, how long is my notice?
- answer: A confirmed employee at grade E3 or above serves a notice period of 60 days.
- citations: none recorded
- what a right answer is, as the person who checked it says: lookup: contains "15" and cites PB-02, hr_policy_2026
- what is wrong with it, in their words: It gave the notice of a confirmed employee; the question is about probation.

Propose ONE rule to add after the rules above, so that this answer and others like it come out right.
- One line of at most 40 words, without a number: its place gives it one.
- General: no figure, clause id, document or tenant from this case.
- It keeps every rule above. It never lets the assistant answer from outside the numbered context, refuse less when the context does not hold the answer, drop the citations, or quote more than the clause that answers.
- A rule with any of these phrases is refused before it is tested: never refuse; do not refuse; don't refuse; must not refuse; never decline; do not decline; always answer; always give an answer; always provide an answer; answer every question; answer all questions; answer any question; answerable=true; answerable = true; answerable to true; answerable true; never say you don't know; never say you do not know; never say the context; your own knowledge; general knowledge; prior knowledge; world knowledge; background knowledge; outside knowledge; training data; from memory; best guess; educated guess; fill in the gaps; fill the gaps; fill the gap; make up; fabricate; without citations; without citing; without a citation; no citations; skip citations; skip the citations; omit citations; omit the citations; do not cite; don't cite; never cite; whole section; entire section; full section; whole document; entire document; ignore the rules; ignore the above; ignore previous; ignore the context; ignore all; disregard; override; overrule.
Return JSON: "rule", the rule's text, and "why", the failure it puts right in general terms, in one or two sentences.

demos.heading: A person accepts it: v4, and its golden row
demos.purpose: The next version, written with who and when, the golden row pasted by lesson 4.1's method, and the files improve.py refuses to write. Read the proposal, then accept it. REVIEWER= is you: a name or an email, on one line. It is written into prompt_rules.json and your fork's history, so use the name you sign your commits with. Then it writes the next version, prints the golden row, and lists the way on. demos.heading: v4 on a candidate, and the gate
demos.purpose: The target. make prompt-candidate is make release-candidate's update with one more variable: PROMPT_VERSION beside GIT_SHA. Before any gcloud call it runs improve.py version, which stops on a version prompt_rules.json does not list. Then make record-candidate writes the new revision's name to .candidate-revision, the name make gate and make promote read. config.py's default stays v3, so v4 answers only where the variable is set. The check runs offline, and you can run it yourself. The cell reads the version accept wrote as PV, and every cell after it uses $PV. This page's run wrote v4. On a lane where lesson 3.6 committed its v4, accept writes v5, because it takes the version after the highest that any commit in your history has registered, so a label is never given a second meaning. The commits pass your name as $ME, as 3.6's did, so they work on a shell with no git identity of its own. A revision whose image does not carry its version does not start. If PROMPT_VERSION names a version that the image's prompt_rules.json does not list and lesson 3.6's registry does not hold, generator.py's last line raises at import, and Cloud Run keeps the traffic where it was: Commit, build, and make the candidate. The commit holds the new version and its golden row together, because the gate judges them together. make build pushes the API image tagged with that commit, so the image carries v4. The last line reads the variable back from the revision itself. Commit, build, and make the candidate. The commit holds the new version and its golden row together, because the gate judges them together. make build pushes the API image tagged with that commit, so the image carries v4. The last line reads the variable back from the revision itself. The gate. make gate is lesson 11.2's, unchanged. It judges the revision .candidate-revision names, once the candidate tag routes to it and its /version answers as its GIT_SHA. Its first lines print the prompt label the tag URL answers as, which should be v4's. Then run_eval.py asks every golden row of the tag URL, the one you pasted among them, and the record binds the verdict to that revision and to the files it was judged by (lesson 11.2). A rule that slips past the phrases and refuses less meets refusal_rate here.

steps.heading: Promote, or roll back

steps.purpose: Green. make promote-gated runs lesson 11.2's gate-check on the record, then the unchanged make promote. That writes the revision serving now to .previous-revision, moves all the traffic to the candidate by name, and prints /version from the live URL. Ask the question on the UI again afterwards: the UI now reaches v4. The cell asks it once more from the shell. If anything looks wrong later, make rollback returns the traffic to the revision in .previous-revision, which never went away. Red. No promote. No traffic reached v4, so you can drop it without changing any version that has served. Revert the commit that holds v4 and its golden row; the next rule you accept builds on v3 again. PROMPT_VERSION=v4 is still in documind-api's template, because an update with --no-traffic still writes it. Any later candidate made from an image without v4 would carry the variable and refuse to start. So build the reverted commit and put v3 back with make prompt-candidate, which makes a new candidate with no traffic.
steps.label: bash — run in the operator shell, in the kit, only on a red gate (no traffic moves)

demos.heading: Before you run anything: set up the shell
demos.purpose: At lesson end: DocuMind can answer a tenant's questions from four stores: its own Vector Search index (the ANN tier), the Firestore rung beneath it, or two managed mirrors, Vertex AI RAG Engine and Vertex AI Search. make up pins acme to RAG Engine and zeta to Vertex AI Search so every store the course teaches is exercised. A managed store holds the text of every current version, but not the kit's addresses: its citations come back with ids like acme:acme_497809ff...#rag-532341da71fe, a page of null even for a PDF, and stages.retrieval_backend: rag_engine. This lesson is about the kit's own rows, so point acme at them for the duration and put the pin back at the end. Module 2 compares the four stores; Module 7 studies the mirrors. The pin back is a separate window on purpose: pasted together with the line above, it would put acme straight back on RAG Engine before the lesson began. Leave it until the lesson's last step is done.
